transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith, welcome in. What brings you here today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thanks for seeing me. Um, yeah, so I'm here because I've just been getting really, really frustrated with myself lately. I recently finished my bachelor's degree, so right now I don't have a job, and I'm basically treating my job hunt and all my next steps as my full-time occupation. I spend hours sitting at my laptop just trying to get my life organized and moving forward. 

But what finally made me actually pick up the phone and come in today is that... well, I just keep turning in applications or compiling my research notes, and they always seem to have these really small but honestly just embarrassing mistakes in them. Like, I'll completely mislabel an artwork date, or I'll just entirely skip a question on an important form. 

And the part that really gets to me, the part that makes me feel like I'm going crazy, is that I honestly thought I had checked them. I will sit there, read through the whole page, tell myself it looks perfect, and hit submit. I really put the effort into proofreading! But then later, I'll look back at the file and the error is just glaring right at me. It's like my brain just completely deleted that line while I was reviewing it. I'm just so tired of looking careless when I'm actually trying really hard, you know? It's just... it's really starting to mess with my confidence, because how am I supposed to get my foot in the door anywhere if I look like I don't care enough to fill out a basic form right?
Have you noticed this pattern of making careless mistakes or losing focus on details going back to childhood or your school years, or is this something that's only started recently?

Oh, no, it's definitely not a new thing. I mean, it's always been there, just... maybe the stakes are higher now so I'm noticing it more? But yeah, if I really think about it, going all the way back to elementary school, this was pretty much my exact reputation. 

I remember my parents going to parent-teacher conferences, or getting my report cards, and it was always the exact same story every single year. The teachers would always write these notes saying, you know, that I was a smart kid, that I had really good ideas in class discussions and I understood the material, but... then they'd point out that I constantly forgot to actually turn in the worksheets we did. Or I'd completely lose the printed instructions for a project before I even got home. It was always these little details that I just totally missed, like forgetting to put my name on the top of the paper or skipping the entire back page of a math test because I just didn't realize I was supposed to flip it over. 

It actually got to the point where, for years, my parents had to physically sit down with me and dump out my backpack every single night. Because if they didn't check it, there would just be this black hole of crumpled up assignments and lost instructions at the bottom of the bag. I'd do the homework, I really would, sitting right there at the kitchen table, but if my mom or dad didn't stand over my shoulder and make sure it actually went into the correct folder, and then make sure that folder went into the backpack... it just wouldn't get turned in. They basically had to act as my quality control. So, yeah, it's been happening for a really long time. It's just incredibly frustrating because even back then, I felt like I was trying my best, but the results just never showed it unless someone else was double-checking my every move.

Aside from these mistakes on tasks, do you find yourself frequently worrying about a lot of different things—like your health, relationships, or finances—even when there's no specific task in front of you?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier in that sense. Like, I don't sit around stressing about my health or anything. I feel fine physically, you know? And relationships... well, my friends are great, my family is really supportive—like I said, they basically kept me afloat through school—so I don't really have any anxiety about that kind of stuff. And finances, I mean, obviously I want a job, which is why I'm treating the job hunt like a full-time gig right now, but I'm not, like, lying awake at night panicking about going broke. I'm lucky enough to be living at home right now while I look for work, so I don't have rent hanging over my head. 

It's really just... the frustration with myself. That's the only thing that really gets to me. It's not a generalized worry about the world or my life falling apart, it's just this incredibly specific, incredibly annoying feeling of like, "Why can't I just do this one simple thing right?" When I'm sitting there staring at a cover letter I just spent three hours on, and I realize I spelled the hiring manager's name wrong after checking it five times... that's what upsets me. But it's not like a constant hum of anxiety in the background when I'm just hanging out or going for a walk or whatever. It's very tied to me trying to execute a task and just... failing at the execution part, despite my best efforts. So, yeah, if I'm not actively trying to get my life organized or fill out applications, my brain isn't really spinning out about health or money or anything like that. I just want to be able to trust my own eyes when I proofread something, you know?

Symptoms are chronic, lifelong inattention (careless mistakes, losing materials, forgetting to turn in work, needing external organization) dating back to elementary school, consistent with predominantly inattentive-type ADHD. Ruling out F41.1.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a lifelong (since elementary school) pattern of inattentive symptoms: careless mistakes despite effort, difficulty sustaining attention to detail, losing important materials/instructions, forgetfulness in daily tasks, and needing external structure (parents managing organization) to complete tasks. These symptoms persist into adulthood, causing functional impairment in academic/occupational functioning (errors on job applications, difficulty completing tasks independently). No hyperactive/impulsive symptoms were elicited, and generalized anxiety was explicitly denied, making GAD unlikely. The clinical picture is best explained by ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation.
